title: What Happens to You in Space Without a Spacesuit?
description:
Movies say you'd explode or freeze solid in seconds. The real answer, pieced together from NASA research and a few frightening accidents, is stranger, and you'd have a little more time than you think.

Sources:
- NASA Imagine the Universe, Ask an Astrophysicist: How would the unprotected human body react to the vacuum of outer space?: https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/ask_astro/space_travel.html
- NASA, What Is a Spacesuit?: https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/what-is-a-spacesuit/
- Astronomy Magazine, Remembering the crew of Soyuz 11: https://astronomy.com/news/2021/06/remembering-the-crew-of-soyuz-11-the-only-astronauts-to-die-in-space

sources.title: NASA Imagine the Universe - Ask an Astrophysicist: unprotected human body in vacuum
Astronomy Magazine - Remembering the crew of Soyuz 11, the only astronauts to die in space

scenes.narration: You're on a spacewalk, and something goes wrong. Your suit is gone. Movies say you'd explode or freeze solid. The truth is stranger.
scenes.headline: SPACE WITHOUT A SUIT

visual.note: astronaut floating outside the space station

scenes.narration: First, why you need a suit at all. NASA calls a spacesuit a one person spacecraft. It holds pressure around your body, supplies the oxygen you breathe, removes the carbon dioxide you exhale, and keeps you from overheating or freezing.
scenes.headline: A ONE-PERSON SPACECRAFT

scenes.narration: It's built for a harsh place. Spacewalk temperatures can swing from about minus two hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit in shadow to two hundred fifty in sunlight. That's why a suit can have as many as sixteen layers, including fabric also used in bulletproof vests.
scenes.headline: UP TO 16 LAYERS

scenes.narration: Now take all of that away, and go second by second. Out there, there's essentially no air pressure at all. Right now, about fourteen and a half pounds of air press on every square inch of your body. Lose that in an instant, and several things start happening at once.
scenes.headline: ZERO PRESSURE

visual.query: Space Environment Simulation Laboratory vacuum chamber Johnson
visual.note: a large NASA vacuum test chamber

scenes.narration: Second zero. The single most important thing you could do is breathe out. If you held your breath, the air in your lungs would expand and could tear the delicate tissue inside. Scuba divers learn the same rule for rising toward the surface.
scenes.headline: STEP ONE: BREATHE OUT
scenes.sub: Holding your breath can tear lungs

visual.query: Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory astronaut training diver

scenes.narration: Over the next few seconds, the air rushes out of your lungs, and something cruel happens. With no air outside, oxygen starts leaving your blood through your lungs instead of entering it. Your brain is now running on whatever oxygen it has left.
scenes.headline: OXYGEN LEAVES YOUR BLOOD

visual.spec: lungs and blood vessels with arrows showing oxygen flowing out of the blood into empty lungs in a vacuum

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the moisture on your tongue starts to bubble, even though it isn't hot. In a vacuum, water boils at far lower temperatures, even the temperature of your own body. NASA's own description says the saliva on your tongue might boil.
scenes.headline: YOUR SALIVA BOILS

visual.spec: chart of water's boiling point dropping as air pressure falls, from 212°F at sea level to body temperature near vacuum

scenes.narration: But your blood doesn't boil. Your skin and blood vessels hold their own pressure, and your blood pressure keeps your blood above the point where it would boil. And no, you do not explode. Skin is remarkably tough and stretchy.
scenes.headline: YOU DON'T EXPLODE

visual.note: astronaut glove against the blackness of space

scenes.narration: What does happen is swelling. Some of the water in your soft tissues can turn to vapor, puffing up your skin and the tissue underneath. Doctors call this ebullism. NASA's description calls the swelling mild and reversible. Your skin keeps you in one piece.
scenes.headline: YOU SWELL INSTEAD

scenes.narration: In nineteen sixty, Air Force pilot Joe Kittinger rode a balloon nearly twenty miles up. One of his gloves failed to pressurize, and his hand swelled up, painful and useless. Once he came back down, it returned to normal.
scenes.headline: A REAL WARNING SIGN

visual.note: a giant balloon rising into the stratosphere

scenes.narration: Around ten to fifteen seconds in, your vision fades and you pass out. Your brain has simply run out of oxygen. In the nineteen sixties, a NASA test subject in a vacuum chamber stayed conscious for about fourteen seconds after his suit leaked.
scenes.headline: ABOUT 15 SECONDS

visual.query: Manned Spacecraft Center vacuum chamber test 1960s

scenes.narration: He could feel and hear the air escaping. His last conscious memory was of the water on his tongue beginning to boil. Technicians repressurized the chamber quickly, and he recovered.
scenes.headline: HIS LAST MEMORY: BOILING SALIVA

visual.note: engineer in a pressure suit during testing

scenes.narration: What about the cold? Space is cold, but it's also empty, and emptiness is a great insulator. That's how a thermos works. With no air to carry heat away, you'd lose warmth slowly, mostly by radiating it. You would not freeze solid in seconds.
scenes.headline: YOU DON'T FREEZE INSTANTLY

scenes.narration: There's a catch, though. The space station circles Earth about every ninety minutes, so you'd swing from blazing sunlight into deep shadow roughly every forty five minutes. Without a suit, there's no insulation, no cooling, and no protection from either extreme.
scenes.headline: SUN TO SHADOW EVERY 45 MINUTES

visual.query: orbital sunrise from International Space Station
visual.note: sunrise over Earth's limb from orbit

scenes.narration: In direct sunlight, the bigger danger is the opposite. Without an atmosphere or a gold coated visor to filter it, raw sunlight would start burning exposed skin. According to NASA, sunburn is one of the problems that begins after about ten seconds.
scenes.headline: INSTANT SUNBURN

scenes.narration: And sunlight isn't the only thing streaming past. Spacesuits also shield astronauts from radiation and from tiny, fast moving specks of space dust. Unprotected, your skin and eyes would take every hit.
scenes.headline: RADIATION AND SPACE DUST

visual.query: micrometeoroid impact damage space station window
visual.note: tiny impact chip on a spacecraft window

scenes.narration: So what's the time limit? NASA's estimate: about half a minute of exposure is unlikely to cause permanent injury. But after perhaps one or two minutes, you are dying. And they admit the exact limits aren't really known. Rescue has to come fast.
scenes.headline: THE TWO-MINUTE LIMIT

scenes.narration: That's why spacewalkers usually work in pairs and stay tethered to the station. If something failed, a partner could haul you back toward the airlock. Thirty seconds can be the difference between a terrifying story and a tragedy.
scenes.headline: NEVER ALONE OUT THERE
scenes.sub: Pairs, tethers, and a nearby airlock

scenes.narration: Sadly, we know this from real history. In June nineteen seventy one, a valve on the Soviet Soyuz eleven capsule sprang open about one hundred miles up, as the crew headed home. The cabin air escaped, and all three cosmonauts died within about two minutes.
scenes.headline: THE SOYUZ 11 TRAGEDY

scenes.narration: They remain the only people known to have died in space itself. Since then, crews launching and landing in Soyuz capsules wear pressure suits, just in case. A suit is the last line of defense if the cabin fails.
scenes.headline: WHY CREWS SUIT UP

visual.note: crew in pressure suits before launch

scenes.narration: You don't even need to reach space for this danger. About twelve miles up, the air pressure is so low that water boils at the temperature of your body. Above that height, even pilots need pressure suits.
scenes.headline: IT STARTS 12 MILES UP

visual.query: ER-2 high altitude pilot pressure suit
visual.note: pilot in a high-altitude pressure suit

scenes.narration: So, out in the vacuum without a suit, you wouldn't explode, boil, or freeze in an instant. You'd have about fifteen seconds of awareness, and maybe a minute or two for someone to save you. That's why every astronaut treats a spacesuit as a spacecraft.
scenes.headline: A SUIT IS A SPACECRAFT

scenes.narration: Follow Cosmic What If for more mind-bending science.
